title: Zobo
author: Jazmine Woodward
desc: A cup of dried hibiscus with ginger, turmeric, clove and cinnamon brought just to the boil, then taken off the heat and steeped up to twelve hours.
longDesc: Zobo is dried hibiscus and the method here is unusual in a useful way: everything goes into the pan cold, comes to the boil, and is then taken straight off the heat to steep for up to twelve hours. The long cold steep rather than a long boil keeps the floral notes that hard boiling strips out. Three cups of pineapple juice go in alongside three of water, with a two-inch knob each of ginger and turmeric, half a teaspoon of clove buds and two cinnamon sticks. Served warm or chilled over ice, it makes five servings.
ingredients: 2 cinnamon sticks, plus more for garnish
steps: Rinse the hibiscus under cool water to remove sediment.
Slice the ginger and turmeric into coins.
Add everything to a small saucepan over medium heat.
Bring to a boil, then remove from the heat.
Serve warm, or chill at least one hour and serve over ice.
chefTips: Boil, then off the heat. The steeping does the extraction, not the boiling — a long hard boil strips the floral character and leaves it flat and tannic.
Up to twelve hours is a long steep and it is worth the wait. Four hours gives you something drinkable; twelve gives you depth.
Rinse the hibiscus first. Dried calyces carry grit and sediment.
Coins, not grated, for the ginger and turmeric. You are infusing and then straining, so you want pieces you can get out.
Pineapple juice is half the liquid here and it is doing the sweetening — which is why no sugar is listed. Add sugar only after tasting.
Turmeric will stain everything it touches, including your hands and a wooden spoon.
The warm service is a declared invention by the author, framed as an Afrofuturist adaptation for different climates. Traditional zobo is served cold.
commonMistakes: Boiling it for twenty minutes instead of steeping.
Grating the ginger and turmeric so they cannot be strained out.
Adding sugar before tasting, when the pineapple juice may be enough.
Steeping it at room temperature for twelve hours in hot weather — refrigerate it instead.
sources: Adapted from 'How to Make Nigerian Zobo Drink (Hot or Iced)', byline Jazzmine Woodard, dashofjazz.com. Headnote as printed: 'West African medicinal drink with floral, earthy, warm, and fruity flavor notes, also known as hibiscus tea.' YIELD AS PRINTED: 5 servings.

Quantities exactly as printed: 1 cup dried hibiscus; 1 two-inch knob of ginger; 1 two-inch knob of turmeric; 3 cups pineapple juice; 3 cups water; 1/2 teaspoon clove buds; 2 cinnamon sticks (plus more for optional garnish).

Method as printed: rinse the hibiscus under cool water to remove sediment; slice the ginger and turmeric into coins; add everything to a small saucepan over medium heat; bring to a boil, then remove from heat; 'Steep up to 12 hours', then strain the solids; serve warm, or chill at least one hour and serve over ice.

AUTHOR-DECLARED DEVIATION, flagged: the WARM preparation is offered alongside the traditional cold or iced serving and is framed by the author herself as an 'Afrofuturism' adaptation for varied global climates. The hot service is therefore NOT traditional, by her own framing, and that is recorded rather than passed off as standard.

No sugar appears in the ingredient list — the pineapple juice is the sweetener. Traditional zobo is usually sweetened separately, often with sugar or with pineapple or ginger, so this is within the normal range of the drink.

A NOTE ON A RELATED DRINK NOT PUBLISHED: Lopè Ariyo's hibiscus chicken (NGA116) uses the same dried petals in a savoury dish, and that recipe is published as a declared invention. Zobo itself is traditional; the warm service here is the only declared departure.

GAPS in the Nigerian drinks record, all specifically sought and all empty of named-source recipes: PALM WINE, BURUKUTU and PITO returned nothing citable. Those are fermentations and none has a documented doneness cue in anything consulted, so none is published here. GARRI AS A DRINK with groundnuts likewise has no quantified named-source recipe.
storage: 5 days refrigerated in a sealed jug.
reheating: Warm gently if serving hot. Do not boil it again.
healthBenefits: Hibiscus is associated in clinical studies with modest reductions in blood pressure.
Very high in vitamin C and anthocyanins.
Ginger and turmeric both have documented anti-inflammatory activity.
culturalNote: Zobo is made from the dried calyces of Hibiscus sabdariffa, the same plant that gives sorrel in the Caribbean, bissap in Senegal and agua de Jamaica in Mexico — one of the clearest single threads running through the Atlantic world's drinks. In Nigeria it is sold in sachets and bottles everywhere, and it is the standard non-alcoholic option at a party.
